sec.title: Background
sec.p: Mpox remains a significant public health threat in Africa, with recent outbreaks driven by newly emergent clades I and II. Vaccination is a critical intervention for outbreak control, yet detailed evidence on vaccine acceptance and uptake across the continent has not been comprehensively synthesized. This study aimed to determine the pooled prevalence and determinants of mpox vaccine acceptance and uptake in Africa during and after the global mpox outbreak.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: We searched PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, Cumulative Index to Nursing and Allied Health Literature (CINAHL), ScienceDirect, and African Journals Online. Studies conducted between 2022 and 2024 were included. Articles available in French and English were considered. A random-effects model was used to pool the estimates. Subgroup analyses explored heterogeneity. Key determinants of vaccine acceptance and uptake were systematically identified from the included report findings.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: The pooled mpox vaccine acceptance rate in Africa was 54.97% (95% confidence interval (CI): 49.22–60.59; 15,613 participants; 22 records, 10 countries) with high heterogeneity (I² = 97.8%; p < 0.001). The pooled willingness to vaccinate differ significantly by participant type (p < 0.001). It was higher among the general population (62.02%; 95% CI: 52.86–70.39; n = 9 records; I² = 98.8%) than among healthcare workers (47.97%; 95% CI: 37.35–58.78; n = 6 records; I² = 97.1%). In contrast, pooled vaccine uptake was low at 3.40% (95% CI: 0.56–17.96; 5,740 participants; 8 records, 10 countries), indicating high heterogeneity (I² = 99.7%; p < 0.001). A significant difference (p < 0.001) was observed between studies conducted in the Central Africa region (2.24%: 95% CI: 0.46–10.14; n = 4 records; I² = 81.6%) and the Western zone (38.13%; 95% CI: 27.21–50.39; n = 2 records; I² = 97.5%). Key factors positively influencing acceptance included higher education, greater mpox knowledge, higher risk perception, and trust in health authorities and vaccine safety.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: There is a substantial gap between mpox vaccine acceptance and actual uptake in Africa. Strategies to enhance vaccination must address both demand and supply challenges as well as equitable distribution. These findings underscore the need for context-specific, multi-level interventions to translate reported willingness into actual vaccine uptake.

sec.title: Background
sec.p: Mpox (monkeypox) is an infectious viral disease caused by the monkeypox virus, a double-stranded DNA virus belonging to the Orthopoxvirus genus within the Poxviridae family. This family also includes the viruses responsible for smallpox (variola), cowpox, and vaccinia [1]. The infection can cause a painful rash, enlarged lymph nodes, and fever [2].

The mpox virus is causing concurrent outbreaks in several African countries [3]. The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) bears the highest global burden, with travel-related cases that can potentially lead to global outbreaks [4, 5]. In August 2024, the Africa Center for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) declared mpox a Public Health Emergency of Continental Security, while the World Health Organization (WHO) previously declared it a Public Health Emergency of International Concern in July 2023. These declarations followed a global outbreak driven by newly emerged, virulent clades I (Ia, Ib) and II (IIa, IIb) of the mpox virus [6, 7]. By June 2025, several African nations had reported recent community transmission of the clade Ib mpox virus [8].

To effectively combat the mpox pandemic, global health authorities have recommended that countries adopt and implement preventive strategies. These strategies include avoiding close skin-to-skin contact with people who have an mpox-like rash, avoiding close contact with animals that could carry the virus, frequently washing hands with soap or an alcohol-based sanitizer, and vaccination [9–11]. Vaccination is considered one of the most effective interventions for preventing and controlling the unprecedented spread of mpox, which has led to a case fatality rate of over 4% in some Sub-Saharan African countries, such as the DRC [4, 12].

To prevent mpox, vaccination is recommended both as a primary preventive measure for high-risk individuals and as post-exposure prophylaxis for known contacts. Following the initial outbreak, global containment efforts have prioritized vaccination to curb the virus’s spread [13]. The JYNNEOS (Bavarian Nordic A/S, Hellerup, Denmark) vaccine, a replication-deficient vaccinia virus vaccine, is currently being used for this purpose. It was approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) after being proven to be the safest available substitute for the previously used ACAM2000 vaccine (Emergent Product Development Gaithersburg Inc., Gaithersburg, Maryland, USA) [14].

The ACAM2000 vaccine was linked to dangerous side effects, including myopericarditis and even death [15, 16]. In contrast, the most frequently reported side effects of the JYNNEOS vaccine were milder and easier to manage, typically including injection site reactions, headache, myalgia, chills, and nausea [17].

Beyond the fear of potential adverse effects, vaccine hesitancy which is recognized as one of the top ten global health threats [18–21], is fueled by misinformation, attitudes and perceptions such as the fear of needles and doubts about a vaccine’s efficacy and usefulness [22, 23]. Additionally, studies in Africa have identified several sociodemographic characteristics associated with vaccine acceptance and uptake [20, 21, 24–27]. Prior to the 2022 global mpox outbreak, mpox vaccine acceptance reported in two studies from the DRC was 18% and 85%, respectively [28, 29], while vaccine uptake ranged from 3% to 94% across various African countries [28–45].

In this regard, the need to develop and implement an mpox vaccination toolkit has become crucial. Such a toolkit offers a set of practical guidance, training, and information resources to help relevant stakeholders in African countries prepare, plan, implement, and monitor mpox vaccination programs [46]. Moreover, community engagement is essential for the successful implementation of these programs. Fostering trust, ensuring cultural sensitivity, tailoring interventions, and building sustainable health systems are key components of a successful vaccination strategy [47]. Key strategies for engagement include involving trusted local actors and community representatives in decision-making, disseminating accessible information through diverse platforms, and actively collecting social and behavioral insights to adapt strategies and combat misinformation [48].

However, the primary challenge to controlling mpox in Africa is the limited access to vaccines, which is hindered by both supply and distribution issues [49]. Another significant challenge is identifying high-risk adults for vaccination, particularly given the sexual transmission of Clade I mpox strains. A third major hurdle is designing and implementing vaccination programs that effectively reach at-risk children under five, who face the highest mortality risk. This challenge is compounded by the need to ensure that their parents are willing to accept vaccination for their children [50].

Several studies conducted in Africa provide insight into the use of the mpox vaccine to combat recurrent outbreaks. These studies indicate varying levels of vaccine acceptance and uptake [25, 28–30, 32, 33, 35–42, 45, 51–53]. In addition, there is a lack of more detailed and granular analysis of specific populations, settings, temporal trends, and country- and region-specific pooled acceptance and coverage rates for the mpox vaccine, as well as the socio-behavioral factors influencing them. This knowledge gap hinders the development of tailored, subregional or country-specific vaccination strategies. To address these limitations, we conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis to estimate the prevalence and synthesize the determinants of mpox vaccine acceptance and uptake across Africa, stratifying by subregion, country, and key populations, including the general public and healthcare workers.

sec.title: Study design
sec.p: This review was reported in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines (Supplementary Material 1: Prisma checklist). It was registered with the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews under the number CRD420251126033 (https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420251126033) [54].

sec.title: Study outcome
sec.p: The primary outcomes of this systematic review and meta-analysis were mpox vaccine acceptance and mpox vaccine uptake. Vaccine acceptance was defined as the unconditional willingness to receive an mpox vaccine if offered [13, 25]. Vaccine uptake was defined as receiving one or more of the vaccines approved for mpox prevention and/or treatment [13, 55].

sec.title: Eligibility criteria
sec.p: This systematic review and meta-analysis included all studies from Africa available online that reported on mpox vaccination uptake and acceptance based on condition, context, and population [56]. Eligible studies included any individuals residing in Africa (the population), assessed either actual mpox vaccine uptake or acceptance (the condition), and were conducted in any African setting, including community, hospital, or online contexts. Accordingly, we included original full-text articles that reported on any of our study’s outcomes of interest: prevalence of mpox vaccine acceptance, vaccination coverage, or factors associated with mpox vaccine acceptance or uptake. Articles available in French and English were included.

We excluded studies that were only available as abstracts or focused solely on conditional acceptance, such as willingness to pay for the vaccine. We also did not include studies that failed to report our primary outcomes, measured outcomes only with continuous variables without providing prevalence or were strictly clinical trials of the mpox vaccine. Finally, we did not include studies conducted before the 2022 global outbreak.

sec.title: Article searching strategy
sec.p: We identified published research through a systematic search of online databases, including PubMed, Scopus, Cumulative Index to Nursing and Allied Health Literature (CINAHL), Web of Science, ScienceDirect, and African Journals Online (AJOL). The search process involved screening titles and abstracts of entries generated after using a combination of keywords and Medical Subject Headings (MeSH). We used Boolean operators like “AND” and “OR” to refine our search with terms such as: mpox OR monkeypox AND vaccine OR vaccination OR acceptance OR willingness OR uptake AND African countries (Supplementary Material 2: Search strategy). To ensure comprehensive coverage, we also conducted a manual search on Google Scholar for publications not indexed in the primary databases and screened the reference lists of all included studies for relevant articles. The screening was conducted by two independent authors (FZLC and CA) and any discrepancies observed were resolved through discussion. The final search was completed on August 07, 2025. Additional search was concluded on December 07, 2025.

sec.title: Data extraction
sec.p: We used Zotero software version 7.0.16 (Corporation for Digital Scholarship, Vienna, Virginia, USA) to retrieve and de-duplicate references from our literature search. One investigator (FZLC) then used a pre-designed Microsoft Excel 2016 form to extract key study characteristics. The form captured the article ID (first author name, country, year of study completion), study year, country, study design, participant type, setting, sampling technique, the number of individuals willing to receive the vaccine, the number who received it, the total sample size and the factors associated with vaccine acceptability and/or uptake. The collected data were then cross-checked by two other investigators (RT and AAN) and any discrepancies during data extraction were solved through discussion to reach consensus.

sec.title: Critical appraisal (quality assessment) of included studies
sec.p: Two authors independently assessed the relevance and quality of each article (FZLC and AC). Any disagreements between the reviewers were resolved through discussion with a third author (MNT) to reach a consensus. The Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) quality assessment tool was used to evaluate the quality of studies included [57]. For cross-sectional studies assessing prevalence, the parameters include appropriateness of the sampling frame, suitable sampling technique, adequate sample size, description of study subjects and setting, sufficient data analysis, use of valid methods for identified conditions, valid measurement for all participants, use of appropriate statistical analysis, and adequate response rate. Each criterion was scored as 1 (yes) or 0 (no or unclear).

sec.title: Statistical analysis and synthesis
sec.p: To explore the variability in results, subgroup analyses were conducted based on several factors: study period, country, study setting (community, hospital, and online), participant type, and sampling technique. Countries were grouped by the WHO African Region (WHO Afro) [58], including the Western (Algeria, Ghana, and Nigeria), Eastern (Ethiopia, Kenya, and Uganda), Southern (South Africa), and Central (Cameroon and the DRC) regions. The analysis also included a non-WHO Afro region (Northern Africa), which comprised Morocco and Egypt.

The I2 statistic was used to assess heterogeneity between studies, with categories defined as low (< 25%), moderate (25–75%), or high (> 75%). A Der Simonian and Laird random-effects model was chosen to pool the estimates and their corresponding confidence intervals (CIs), anticipating significant heterogeneity. The generalized linear mixed models (GLMM), coupled with the probit-logit transformation (PLOGIT), were utilized for their effectiveness in handling meta-analyses of binary data and accommodating studies with 0% or 100% event rates without requiring continuity corrections [59]. Statistical significance was set at a p-value of < 0.05. All analyses were conducted using the ‘meta’ package in R Statistics version 4.5.2 (R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria) [60]. Correlates to willingness to receive the vaccine and vaccine uptake were synthesized from the existing literature and narratively presented.

sec.title: Publication bias and sensitivity analysis
sec.p: To evaluate potential publication bias among the included studies, we used funnel plots. The symmetry of the inverted funnel shape suggested the absence of publication bias. In addition, statistical evaluation was conducted using Egger’s linear regression test and Begg’s rank correlation test [61, 62]. A p-value > 0.05 indicated no statistically significant evidence of publication bias. The trim-and-fill method was used to adjust for potential publication bias. Sensitivity analysis was conducted by iteratively excluding one study at a time to assess the robustness of the findings.

sec.title: Characteristics of studies included
sec.p: A total of 10,098 entries were obtained through an online database search and a manual search. After removing 762 duplications, 9336 distinct entries underwent title and abstract review, followed by a complete text evaluation for suitability. Ultimately, 20 research papers met the inclusion criteria and were included in the meta-analysis (Fig. 1).

sec.p: This analysis of mpox vaccination studies available online between 2023 and 2025 across Africa reveals several key patterns. The evidence base was dominated by cross-sectional studies (20/20 = 100% of included studies) [17, 25–27, 51–53, 55, 64–75], primarily focused on the Nigeria (4/20 = 20% of studies) [72, 73, 75, 76], with most (13/20 = 65%) using non-probabilistic sampling methods) [17, 25, 51, 53, 55, 64–68, 71, 73, 74]. Reports describe vaccine acceptance specifically [17, 25, 26, 51, 64, 65, 67–69, 71, 73–75] and uptake [51–53, 66] outcomes or both [27, 55, 70, 72], with studies targeting the general population (8/20 = 40%) [25, 27, 51–53, 55, 65, 66, 74] and online data collection (8/20 = 40%) [26, 55, 64, 65, 68, 71, 74, 77]. Most studies were rated low risk of bias (87%) [17, 26, 27, 52, 53, 55, 66–75] (Table 1).

sec.title: Mpox vaccine acceptance
sec.p: This meta-analysis reveals moderate overall mpox vaccine acceptance in Africa at 54.97% (95% CI: 49.22–60.59; 15,613 participants; n = 22 records), with high heterogeneity (I²=97.8%; p <0.001), indicating significant variation between studies. The highest prevalence was observed in a study conducted in Egypt (78%; 95% CI : 73.05–82.68; 302 participants ) [29] and lowest in Ethiopia (28.84%; 95% CI: 25.62–32.23; 749 participants) [26] (Fig. 2).

sec.p: While some countries like South Africa (67.43%; 95% CI: 61.85–72.67; 304 participants; n = 1 report), Uganda (62.95%; 95% CI: 57.26–68.39; 305 participants; n = 1 report) [55] showed relatively highest acceptance, others such as and Ghana (42.27%; 95% CI: 27.82–58.17; 2,664 participants; n = 2 report) [17, 27], Algeria (44.98%; 95% CI: 37.64–52.55; 303 participants; n = 2 reports) [64, 65] and Ethiopia (48.53%; 95% CI: 29.57–67.92; 1,333 participants; n = 3 reports) [26, 69, 70] demonstrated lower rates. There was a significant difference between subgroup pooled estimates between countries (p = 0.001) and WHO Afro zones (p = 0.023). The pooled prevalence of vaccine acceptance was higher among individuals in the general population (62.02%; 95% CI: 52.86–70.39; 9,269 participants; n = 9 reports) than among healthcare workers (47.97%; 95% CI: 37.35–58.78; 2,855 participants; n = 6 reports). A high level of heterogeneity was observed in most subgroups, indicating substantial variation between studies ( Table 2 and Supplementary Material 3: Fig. S 1–8).

sec.title: Mpox vaccine uptake
sec.p: The pooled vaccination coverage in Africa was 3.40% (95% CI: 0.56-17.96; 5,740 participants; n = 8 reports) demonstrating high heterogeneity (I² = 99.7%, p <0.001) (Fig 3).

sec.p: The subgroup analysis of mpox vaccination uptake in Africa reveals disparities across countries; ranging from 0% in Ethiopia (95% CI: 0.00-0.96; 384 participants; n = 1 report) and DRC (95% CI : 0.00-1.52; 241 participants, n = 1 reports) [53, 70] to 47.21% in Nigeria (42.08–52.39; 377 participants; n = 1 reports) [72]. The significant subgroup differences (p < 0.001) highlighted that geographic location influenced vaccination uptake. In this regard, compared to Central Africa (2.24%; 95% CI: 0.46–10.14; 1,097 participants; n = 4 reports), studies from Western Africa reported a significantly higher mpox vaccine uptake (38.13%; 95% CI: 27.21–50.39; 2,436 participants; n = 2 reports) (Table 3 and Supplementary Material 4: Fig. S 11–17).

sec.title: Publication bias and sensitivity test analysis
sec.p: The funnel plot assessing publication bias for the pooled prevalence of mpox vaccine acceptance, showed a slight shift of the funnel plot, suggesting potential publication bias. However, Egger’s test (p = 0.865) and Begg’s test (p = 0.205) did not indicate any statistically significant bias (Additional Files 2, Supplementary Fig. 9). The sensitivity analysis showed that no study significantly influences the pooled estimate of the vaccine acceptance rate reflecting the robustness of the finding (Supplementary Material 3: Fig. S 9–10).

The analysis revealed significant publication bias in mpox vaccine uptake studies from Africa, evidenced by funnel plot asymmetry. The initial random-effects model showed a pooled prevalence of mpox vaccine uptake of 3.4% (95% CI: 0.56–17.96, n = 8 reports) while trim-and-fill analysis imputed four missing studies (all with higher uptake estimates > 70%), adjusting the pooled rate to 23.51% (95% CI: 4.79–65.26). However, the high heterogeneity (I² = 98.5%) suggests the adjusted estimate may overcorrect due to fundamental differences in study designs/populations rather than pure publication bias. The sensitivity analysis showed that no study significantly influences the pooled estimate of the vaccine uptake rate reflecting the robustness of the finding (Supplementary Material 4: Fig. S 18–20).

sec.title: Factors associated with mpox vaccine acceptance and uptake
sec.p: The synthesis of included studies assessing vaccine acceptance and uptake identified several factors. These factors included:

Age. Vaccine uptake was linked to age, with individuals 15 years and older more likely to be vaccinated [31, 33, 34]. A higher vaccination rate was also associated with being 20 years of age or older [32, 36, 38], while another study found a positive association with an age exceeding 33 years [28].
Sexe. Vaccine uptake was higher in men [31], and gender was also associated with vaccine acceptance [26, 27, 73].
Income. Having a higher income has been linked to both a higher likelihood of vaccine acceptance [72] and a lower likelihood of it [27].
Good mpox knowledge. Higher mpox knowledge was linked to greater vaccine acceptance [17, 64, 65, 68, 70].
Education. Higher education levels is associated with increased vaccine acceptance [70–72].
Risks perception. Risk perception is also linked to greater vaccine acceptance [26, 64, 65, 68].
Trust in authorities and healthcare system. Trust in governmental and healthcare institutions constituted a significant factor in vaccine adoption [26, 64, 72].
Mpox vaccine trust. Trusting the mpox vaccine to be safe is associated with higher acceptance [26, 28, 29, 64, 65].
Mpox-related information. Receiving mpox information from health authorities was linked to a higher likelihood of vaccine acceptance [25, 28, 29].
Social norms and influences. Positive recommendations from social circles, including peers and close contacts, were associated with a greater willingness to get vaccinated [17, 29].
Previous vaccination history. A prior vaccination history, such as having received a COVID-19 or influenza vaccine, was a significant predictor of mpox vaccine acceptance [27, 64, 67, 68].
Localization. Residents in urban settings are significantly more likely to accept vaccination [26, 72].
Education and training. Receiving specific training about mpox and vaccination increased willingness to vaccinate [17, 67].
Perceived mpox susceptibility. The perception of being highly susceptible or at risk of mpox has been associated with a higher likelihood of willingness to receive the mpox vaccine [29].
Family history of mpox. Families with a history of severe mpox cases demonstrated higher risk perception and greater vaccine acceptance [65].

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: This systematic review and meta-analysis provide insights on mpox vaccine acceptance and uptake in Africa from the 2022 global outbreak onward. Our results, considered from both African and international viewpoints, show a moderate willingness to vaccinate (54.97%). However, this estimate should be interpreted with caution given the significant heterogeneity among the included studies (I² = 97.8%; p < 0.001). The acceptance rate we found is similar to global meta-analyses, which reported rates between 56% and 59% [13, 78, 79]. This suggests that vaccine hesitancy toward mpox is a global issue, not just an African one. Subgroup analyses showed that mpox vaccine acceptance in Africa varies by time, location, population group, and study methods. There were also significant differences by country (p < 0.001) and by WHO African subregions (p = 0.023), but not between WHO Afro and non-Afro countries (p = 0.792). Higher acceptance in Southern and Central Africa, especially in South Africa and the DRC, may be due to more exposure to mpox outbreaks and greater familiarity with Orthopoxvirus infections in these areas. Differences in healthcare systems may also play a role [29, 80]. In contrast, lower acceptance in countries such as Ghana, Algeria, and Ethiopia may be due to less direct exposure to mpox, lower perceived risk, and competing public health priorities [69, 81]. There were also clear differences between participant groups (p < 0.001). Acceptance was higher among the general population and people living with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), but lower among healthcare workers and medical students. Previous studies have found that healthcare workers often have more concerns about vaccine safety, less local evidence, or uncertainty about changing recommendations [82, 83]. Higher acceptance among people living with HIV may be because they feel more vulnerable to infectious diseases, which is known to affect vaccine decisions [84]. Differences between study settings were not statistically significant (p = 0.645), but community-based studies tended to show lower acceptance than hospital-based or online surveys. Studies using non-probabilistic sampling reported higher acceptance than those using probabilistic methods, though this was not statistically significant (p = 0.063). These patterns likely contributed to the high heterogeneity observed across subgroupsAlthough mpox vaccine acceptance was moderate, actual vaccine uptake in Africa after the 2022 outbreak was very low, with pooled coverage at 3.40%, this significant gap between willingness and actual vaccination shows that acceptance has not led to widespread coverage. The very high variability between settings (I² = 99.7%) means the pooled estimate should be viewed with caution [85]. Uptake differed by location, from 0% in some studies conducted in Ethiopia and the DRC to almost 50% in Nigeria, with higher coverage in Western Africa than in Central and Eastern Africa. Differences across participant groups, study settings, and sampling methods were not significant, and uptake remained, even among healthcare workers. These results suggest that structural and supply-side barriers, not lack of acceptance, were the main reasons for low mpox vaccination in Africa [80, 86, 87]. In this regard, some authors have raised concerns about mpox vaccine supply and availability in sub-Saharan Africa, where a critical shortage of vaccines and antivirals has fueled mpox outbreaks in several African countries, such as Sierra Leone, Uganda, and the DRC [88]. Moreover, a systematic review revealed that Africa continues to depend on external vaccine sources, a situation shaped by weak local pharmaceutical systems. Although efforts to establish local manufacturing are emerging, several constraints have been identified as barriers to their effective expansion. Such barriers include limited infrastructure, fragmented regulatory systems, shortages of skilled workers, and restrictive intellectual property regimes. Ultimately, the review underscores the necessity of harmonizing regulatory frameworks and securing sustainable investment to bolster regional manufacturing capacity [89]. Nevertheless, some authors have raised concerns about the consequences of overreliance on expert-driven mass vaccination strategies at the expense of more diversified, context-specific, and systemic public health approaches. The reasons highlighted include the fact that Congolese populations face far more pressing health burdens. In a context of limited resources, they suggest that locally owned public health strategies and sanitation approaches are essential [90]. Our study found that sociodemographic, socioeconomic, and educational factors influenced vaccine acceptance and uptake. Higher education was consistently linked to a greater willingness to vaccinate [70–72], supporting earlier research that health literacy increases vaccine confidence [91]. However, the effects of income were contradictory: higher income was associated with both greater [72]. and lower acceptance [27]. These inconsistencies likely reflect contextual differences, as wealth may improve access in some settings but coincide with skepticism of government or donor-driven campaigns in others [92]. Beyond formal education, knowledge about mpox, risk perception, and perceived susceptibility were strongly associated with acceptance [17, 64, 68, 70]. This aligns with the Health Belief Model, where perceived risk drives preventive health behavior [93]. Additionally, training interventions [17, 67] boosted willingness, echoing evidence from Ebola and COVID-19 vaccination programs in Africa, where targeted education improved uptake [94]. Trust and information emerged as central themes. Confidence in health authorities and the healthcare system [26, 64, 72], and trust in the vaccine’s safety [26, 28, 29, 64], were critical drivers, consistent with global evidence that institutional trust underpins vaccine confidence [95]. Conversely, mistrust has repeatedly undermined campaigns during Ebola and coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) outbreaks [96]. Receiving information from health authorities increased acceptance [25, 28, 29], while social influences such as peer and family recommendations also shaped decisions [17, 29]. A prior vaccination history, including for COVID-19 or influenza, predicted acceptance [27, 64, 67, 68], suggesting that established immunization habits carry over to new vaccines [97]. Structural barriers were equally important: free provision [17, 25] and urban residence [26, 72] increased uptake, while rural populations faced greater challenges, consistent with long-standing inequities in African immunization programs [98]. Finally, a family history of mpox increased both risk perception and acceptance [64], mirroring Ebola outbreaks where personal experience heightened demand [99]. Overall, these findings suggest that improving mpox vaccine uptake in Africa will need efforts at many levels. This includes addressing structural barriers to access such as improving the Africa manufacturing capability for vaccines and other emergency required-medical supplies, tailoring education and communication for different groups, building trust with clear messaging, and using lessons from previous vaccination campaigns. Because individual, social, and systemic factors all play a role, strategies must be adapted to local contexts to make sure acceptance leads to fair and widespread uptakeThis review has several limitations such as the small sample sizes in some subgroup analyses resulted in wide confidence intervals, limiting the precision of the findings. The restriction to French or English articles might have limited the number of primary studies included. The predominance of non-probabilistic surveillance data might limit the inference. In addition, the vaccination status relied primarily on individual reports instead of the presentation of a vaccination card testifying to the reception of the vaccine.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: This systematic review and meta-analysis provide a comprehensive synthesis of Mpox vaccination trends in Africa, offering valuable insights into temporal patterns, geographic disparities, and implementation gaps through robust analysis. The study revealed Mpox vaccine acceptance in Africa remains moderate overall (55%) but highly heterogeneous across countries, regions, and population groups. While willingness to vaccinate often approaches or exceeds global averages, actual coverage is markedly lower (3%), highlighting fragility in vaccine supply and delivery systems. The pronounced acceptance–uptake gap, especially among healthcare workers and in high-risk settings, underscores that generating demand is only part of the solution. Achieving effective mpox vaccination coverage will require sustained political commitment, equitable and reliable vaccine supply chains, targeted communication strategies, and integration into routine immunization in the most endemic countries.
